prompt: How does an IPv6 static route differ from an IPv4 static route?
options: IPv6 routes use dotted-decimal subnet masks.
IPv4 static routes must always use link-local next hops.
IPv6 uses prefix/length and scopes link-local next hops by interface.
IPv6 route commands select a source rather than a destination.
explanation: IPv6 routes use prefix/length notation, and a link-local next hop needs an exit interface.

whyWrong.0: Dotted-decimal masks are IPv4 notation.
whyWrong.1: IPv4 static routes do not require link-local next hops.
whyWrong.3: A static route names the destination network, not a packet source.

prompt: In S 2001:DB8:20::/64 [1/0], what are the bracketed numbers?
options: Administrative distance 1 and metric 0
Metric 1 and administrative distance 0
One route advertisement and zero errors
One next-hop router and zero alternate paths
explanation: IOS shows [administrative distance/metric]. A static route has distance 1.

whyWrong.1: The order is distance first, then metric.
whyWrong.2: The brackets are not counters.
whyWrong.3: The brackets do not count next hops or paths.

prompt: What does the installed static entry say?
options: The remote /64 uses fe80::2 on Gi0/0 with distance 1.
The /64 has a hop count of 1 and a loss count of 0.
The route describes R1's own local /128 address.
The route applies only to a host whose suffix is ::2.
explanation: The remote /64 is reached through fe80::2 on Gi0/0 with administrative distance 1.

whyWrong.1: The brackets are distance and metric, not hop count and loss.
whyWrong.2: An S /64 is a remote network route, not a local /128.
whyWrong.3: fe80::2 is the next hop, not the destination.

prompt: Which global command enables IPv6 forwarding between interfaces on a router?
options: ipv6 enable
ipv6 unicast-routing
ip routing
ipv6 address autoconfig
explanation: ipv6 unicast-routing enables IPv6 forwarding on the router.

whyWrong.0: ipv6 enable is an interface command and does not enable forwarding.
whyWrong.2: ip routing enables IPv4 forwarding.
whyWrong.3: ipv6 address autoconfig is an interface command that builds an address.

prompt: An IOS router has IPv6 addresses on its interfaces but no ipv6 unicast-routing. Which TWO statements are true?
options: It can answer a directly attached host pinging its own interface address.
It forwards packets between its IPv6 interfaces normally.
It does not provide the required inter-interface IPv6 forwarding.
Its interface IPv6 addresses must immediately be erased.
explanation: Without ipv6 unicast-routing, the router answers pings to its own addresses but does not forward IPv6 between interfaces.

whyWrong.1: Forwarding needs ipv6 unicast-routing.
whyWrong.3: Addresses stay configured; only forwarding is off.

prompt: R1 has a distance-1 primary and a distance-5 backup. The table shows the backup installed. What does this establish?
options: The primary cable is certainly unplugged.
The backup has exactly five intermediate hops.
The backup is selected; the cause needs more evidence.
The backup is only configured and cannot forward traffic.
explanation: The backup is the selected route. The table alone does not show why the primary is missing.

whyWrong.0: The primary could be missing for other reasons, such as a down interface or unresolved next hop.
whyWrong.1: 5 is an administrative distance, not a hop count.
whyWrong.3: An installed route is used for forwarding.

prompt: Neighbor fe80::2 is on R1 Gi0/0. Which command routes 2001:db8:20::/64 through it?
options: ipv6 route 2001:db8:20::/64 gigabitethernet0/0 fe80::2
ip route 2001:db8:20::/64 gigabitethernet0/0 fe80::2
ipv6 route fe80::2/128 gigabitethernet0/0 2001:db8:20::
explanation: A link-local next hop needs an exit interface, so the command has the prefix, the interface, then the next hop.

whyWrong.0: A link-local next hop without an interface is incomplete.
whyWrong.2: ip route is the IPv4 command.
whyWrong.3: This routes the neighbor address instead of the remote LAN.

exhibit.title: Representative IOS excerpt
exhibit.text:
R1(config)# ipv6 route 2001:db8:20::/64 fe80::2
The command is rejected; exact error text varies by image.

prompt: What is missing from the shown command?
options: The command must include the source LAN prefix before its destination prefix.
A link-local next hop can never carry routed traffic.
The link-local next hop needs its exit interface.
The neighbor hardware address must be appended to the route.
explanation: A link-local address is only meaningful on one link, so the route must name the exit interface.

whyWrong.0: Static routes match the destination, not a source.
whyWrong.1: A link-local next hop works when paired with the interface.
whyWrong.3: ND resolves the MAC address; you do not enter it.

exhibit.title: Representative IOS excerpt
exhibit.text:
Primary: R1 Gi0/0 fe80::1 — R2 Gi0/0 fe80::2
Backup: R1 Gi0/1 fe80::1 — R2 Gi0/1 fe80::3
Remote LAN behind R2: 2001:db8:20::/64

prompt: R1 must reach the remote LAN through R2 on the primary link. Which command is correct?
options: ipv6 route 2001:db8:20::/64 gigabitethernet0/0 fe80::1
ipv6 route 2001:db8:20::/64 gigabitethernet0/1 fe80::2
ipv6 route 2001:db8:20::/64 gigabitethernet0/0 fe80::2
explanation: R2 is fe80::2 on the primary link, which is R1 Gi0/0.

whyWrong.0: fe80::1 is R1 itself.
whyWrong.1: Gi0/1 is the backup link, not the link to the primary R2 address.
whyWrong.2: A link-local next hop needs an interface.

prompt: Which command adds an IPv6 default route through 2001:db8:12::2?
explanation: ::/0 matches every IPv6 address, so it is the default route.

whyWrong.0: ::/128 matches one address, not all.
whyWrong.1: 0.0.0.0/0 is the IPv4 default.
whyWrong.2: ip route is the IPv4 command.

prompt: A /64 route uses Gi0/0. Only 2001:db8:20::12 should use backup neighbor fe80::3 on Gi0/1. Which command does that?
options: ipv6 route 2001:db8:20::/64 gigabitethernet0/1 fe80::3
ipv6 route 2001:db8:20::12/128 gigabitethernet0/1 fe80::3
ipv6 route ::/0 gigabitethernet0/1 fe80::3
ipv6 route 2001:db8:20::12/64 gigabitethernet0/1 fe80::3
explanation: A /128 host route matches one address and wins over the /64 by longest prefix match.

whyWrong.0: This competes with the /64 for the whole network.
whyWrong.2: A default route loses to the /64 match.
whyWrong.3: A /64 with a host address is not a host route.

exhibit.title: Representative IOS excerpt
exhibit.text:
ipv6 route 2001:db8:20::/64 GigabitEthernet0/0 FE80::2
ipv6 route 2001:db8:20::/64 GigabitEthernet0/1 FE80::3 5

prompt: Both links are usable. Which TWO statements follow from the configured routes?
options: The primary is preferred because its ordinary distance is 1.
The distance-5 route forwards half the traffic while the primary is installed.
The backup can become selected if the preferred route is withdrawn.
Distance 5 means the backup traverses five routers.
explanation: Lower administrative distance wins, so the distance-1 route is preferred. The distance-5 route is a backup used if the primary is withdrawn.

whyWrong.1: Different distances give a primary and a standby, not load sharing.
whyWrong.3: 5 is an administrative distance, not a router count.

exhibit.title: Representative IOS excerpt
exhibit.text:
::/0 via Gi0/0, distance 1
2001:db8:20::/64 via Gi0/1, distance 1
2001:db8:20::12/128 via Gi0/2, distance 200

prompt: All displayed routes are installed. Which interface forwards traffic to 2001:db8:20::12?
options: Gi0/2, because the /128 is the longest match
Gi0/1, because its distance is less than 200
Gi0/0, because a default takes priority
All three, because the address matches all three
explanation: Routers choose the longest matching prefix first, so the /128 wins. Distance is compared only between routes to the same prefix.

whyWrong.1: Distance is not compared across different prefix lengths.
whyWrong.2: A default route is the least specific match.
whyWrong.3: Only the longest match forwards.

prompt: R1 cannot resolve fe80::2 on Gi0/1, but another cache entry shows fe80::2 on Gi0/0. What should you check?
options: Use the Gi0/0 binding automatically for all interfaces.
Verify whether the intended peer actually owns fe80::2 on the Gi0/1 link.
Assume the repeated address proves global routing is disabled.
Delete all IPv6 routes because a neighbor state is not REACH.
explanation: A link-local address belongs to one link. Verify that the peer on Gi0/1 owns fe80::2.

whyWrong.0: A neighbor on Gi0/0 cannot serve as a next hop on Gi0/1.
whyWrong.2: The evidence concerns one neighbor, not global forwarding.
whyWrong.3: A neighbor state other than REACH is not a reason to delete routes.

exhibit.title: Representative IOS excerpt
exhibit.text:
interface GigabitEthernet0/0
 ipv6 address 2001:db8:12::1/64
!
ipv6 route 2001:db8:20::/64 GigabitEthernet0/0
Remote PC 2001:db8:20::12 is behind R2, not on this transit link.

prompt: R2 owns the remote LAN. Why is an interface-only static route to it a poor choice on Ethernet?
options: It attempts discovery for the remote host on the transit link.
It causes R1 to ask ARP for the remote IPv6 host.
The interface-only form automatically discovers the correct remote router through RA.
The Ethernet interface supplies the remote PC MAC without Neighbor Discovery.
explanation: With no next hop, R1 treats the remote host as on-link and sends Neighbor Discovery for it. Nothing on the transit link answers.

whyWrong.1: IPv6 uses Neighbor Discovery, not ARP.
whyWrong.2: An interface-only route does not name the next-hop router.
whyWrong.3: Ethernet still needs ND to find the MAC.

prompt: Which statement about show ipv6 neighbors is correct?
options: STALE means the entry has not been confirmed recently; it is not a fault.
An empty cache proves the configured peer is absent from the link.
One INCOMPLETE entry proves the entire remote LAN is unreachable permanently.
STALE means the address is duplicated and must be reassigned.
explanation: STALE means the entry has not been confirmed recently, and it is normal. An entry stuck in INCMP while pings fail points to a wrong next hop or interface.

whyWrong.1: The cache holds only discovered neighbors.
whyWrong.2: INCMP can be temporary while resolution runs.
whyWrong.3: STALE is a reachability state, not a duplicate-address result.

prompt: Which TWO observations make repeated FE80::2 next hops unambiguous?
options: Both routes use the same address text, so they must point to one physical router.
Neighbor entries can be combined without keeping their interface field.
The router must replace one link-local address with a global address.
Each route supplies its own local exit interface.
FE80::2 is verified on the adjacent peer interface of each separate link.
explanation: The same link-local address can exist on separate links. The route and the neighbor entry must each keep the interface.

whyWrong.0: The same text does not mean the same router.
whyWrong.1: The interface is needed to tell neighbors apart.
whyWrong.2: A scoped link-local next hop does not need a global address.

exhibit.title: Repeated link-local next hops (exercise)
exhibit.text:
ipv6 route 2001:db8:21:1::/64 Gi0/0 FE80::2
ipv6 route 2001:db8:21:2::/64 Gi0/1 FE80::2
Gi0/0 and Gi0/1 connect to different routed links.

prompt: Which installed route carries a packet to 2001:db8:44:ab3d::8?
options: 2001:db8:44:ab30::/61 through FE80::4 on Gi0/2
2001:db8:44:ab38::/61 through FE80::3 on Gi0/1
2001:db8:44:ab30::/60 through FE80::2 on Gi0/0
::/0 through FE80::5 on Gi0/3
explanation: ab3d falls in ab38 to ab3f, so the /61 matches. Longest prefix match decides before distance.

whyWrong.0: That /61 covers ab30 to ab37.
whyWrong.2: The /60 matches, but the /61 is more specific.
whyWrong.3: The default is the least specific match.

prompt: The temporary /128 is removed. Which route now matches that destination?
options: The installed /64 network route.
No route, because deleting a host route also deletes its containing network route.
The default, because it has lower distance than the /64.
A local L route, because every deleted static becomes local.
explanation: The next longest installed match is the /64. Removing one static route does not remove others.

whyWrong.1: Deleting the /128 leaves the /64 in place.
whyWrong.2: The /64 is more specific than the default.
whyWrong.3: Local routes cover this router's own addresses.

exhibit.title: Routes before exact cleanup (exercise)
exhibit.text:
Before cleanup:
S 2001:db8:24::44/128 [50/0] via FE80::3, Gi0/1
S 2001:db8:24::/64 [20/0] via FE80::2, Gi0/0
S ::/0 [1/0] via FE80::4, Gi0/2
Only the /128 configuration is removed.

exhibit.title: Representative IOS excerpt
exhibit.text:
PC-A: 2001:db8:10::11 behind R1
PC-B: 2001:db8:20::12 behind R2
Complete relevant R2 unicast routes; no default:
C 2001:DB8:12::/64, Gi0/0
L 2001:DB8:12::2/128, Gi0/0
C 2001:DB8:20::/64, Gi0/2
L 2001:DB8:20::1/128, Gi0/2

prompt: All links work and R1 has a route to PC-B's LAN. Which missing route stops replies from reaching PC-A?
options: An R1 route to R2's already connected transit prefix
An R2 host route to its own LAN address
An R2 route to LAN 20 through its own local interface address
An R2 route covering 2001:db8:10::/64 through R1
explanation: Replies are addressed to PC-A in 2001:db8:10::/64, and R2 has no route to that prefix.

whyWrong.0: R1 already has its connected transit prefix.
whyWrong.1: R2 already owns its LAN address.
whyWrong.2: LAN 20 is already local to R2.

prompt: Why does the standby path already carry traffic for 2001:db8:18::25?
options: The host route is used only after Neighbor Discovery on the /64 fails.
The /64 primary must have been removed because the /128 appears.
All distance-50 statics automatically override distance-1 statics.
The /128 is more specific; distance 50 does not make it a standby for the /64.
explanation: A /128 is more specific than the /64, so longest prefix match picks it. A higher distance only makes a route a standby for the same prefix.

whyWrong.0: The /128 wins at route lookup, before any ND failure.
whyWrong.1: Routes of different lengths coexist.
whyWrong.2: Lower distance wins only between routes to the same prefix.

exhibit.title: Network and host route overlap (exercise)
exhibit.text:
Both interfaces are up and both next hops resolve.
S 2001:db8:18::/64 [1/0] via FE80::2, Gi0/0
S 2001:db8:18::25/128 [50/0] via FE80::3, Gi0/1

prompt: The configured static does not install. What should you check first?
options: A usable route resolving 2001:db8:120::2 without circular dependence.
A matching IPv4 static route to the same last two address groups.
A host route to every address inside the destination /64.
A MAC address written directly into the ipv6 route command.
explanation: A next-hop-only route installs only if the router has a route to the next hop. The connected prefix shown does not cover 2001:db8:120::2.

whyWrong.1: IPv4 routes do not resolve IPv6 next hops.
whyWrong.2: One network route covers the whole LAN.
whyWrong.3: You do not enter a MAC in the route; ND resolves it.

exhibit.title: Recursive next-hop reachability (exercise)
exhibit.text:
Configured: ipv6 route 2001:db8:20::/64 2001:db8:120::2
Only connected transit prefix: 2001:db8:12::/64
No other route to 2001:db8:120::2 and no default.
The desired remote /64 is absent from the installed table.

prompt: What does the redundant design lack?
options: A higher distance on R1 primary so that it never returns.
A second copy of R1 backup route with the same values.
A default gateway on R1 pointing at PC-A.
A usable backup return route on R2 to PC-A LAN.
explanation: Traffic needs a backup path in both directions, and R2 has no backup return route to PC-A's LAN.

whyWrong.0: This does not give R2 a return route.
whyWrong.1: R1 already has its backup; a copy changes nothing.
whyWrong.2: PC-A is not a next-hop router.

exhibit.title: Forward and return routes after failure (exercise)
exhibit.text:
Primary directly cabled link fails; backup link and both LANs remain up.
R1 now installs LAN-B /64 via the backup.
R2 lost its only route to LAN-A /64; it has no default.
Both PCs retain their correct on-link gateways.
PC-A to PC-B still fails.

prompt: What follows from this failed remote ping?
options: The backup must install whenever any destination stops replying.
An ordinary static route can remain selected while a failure beyond its usable next hop breaks delivery.
A reachable next hop proves the remote LAN and its return route work.
Reducing both route distances to 1 creates reliable failure detection.
explanation: A static route stays installed while its next hop is usable, even if the path beyond it is broken. Static routes do not check end-to-end delivery.

whyWrong.0: A static route does not monitor destinations.
whyWrong.2: A reachable next hop says nothing about the far LAN or the return path.
whyWrong.3: Changing distance does not detect failures.

exhibit.title: Remote failure with an installed primary (exercise)
exhibit.text:
Primary and backup statics cover the same /64 at distances 1 and 20.
Primary exit interface is up; its connected next hop still answers.
The installed route remains the primary.
A remote failure beyond that neighbor prevents replies; no tracking is configured.

prompt: The endpoint ping fails but the explicitly sourced router ping works. Which return route is missing?
options: R2 needs a route covering 2001:db8:12::1, the connected transit source.
R2 needs a route covering 2001:db8:10::11, the client source.
PC-A should use R2 remote-LAN address as an on-link gateway.
R1 needs another route to 2001:db8:20::/64, the already covered destination.
explanation: The tests use different sources. R2 reaches the transit source by its connected route but has no route to PC-A's LAN.

whyWrong.0: R2 already has the connected transit prefix.
whyWrong.2: The remote address is not on PC-A's link.
whyWrong.3: The outbound route already covers the destination.

exhibit.title: Two ping sources and the return table (exercise)
exhibit.text:
R1: LAN 2001:db8:10::/64; transit 2001:db8:12::1/64
R2: transit 2001:db8:12::2/64; LAN 2001:db8:20::/64
R1 has a route to LAN 20. R2 has only those two connected prefixes.
R1 ping to LAN-20 host with explicit source 2001:db8:12::1 succeeds.
PC-A 2001:db8:10::11 uses its correct local R1 gateway; the same destination test fails.

prompt: The selected /128 host route has a next hop that cannot be resolved. What happens to packets for that host?
options: Packets to that host are dropped; the router does not fall back to the /64 route.
The default route automatically replaces the /128 for that packet.
The router automatically forwards the same packet using the /64 because it has lower distance.
The neighbor failure proves that the destination host itself is powered off.
explanation: The router picks the /128 as the longest match. If its next hop cannot be resolved, the router drops the packet and does not fall back to the /64.

whyWrong.1: The default is less specific than the /128.
whyWrong.2: Longest match is chosen first, and a /64 is not a fallback.
whyWrong.3: The failure is the next hop, not the host.

exhibit.title: Selected host route and unresolved neighbor (exercise)
exhibit.text:
S 2001:db8:23::/64 [1/0] via FE80::2, Gi0/0
S 2001:db8:23::50/128 [200/0] via FE80::9, Gi0/1
After repeated traffic, FE80::9 cannot resolve on Gi0/1.
The /128 remains installed; the /64 path is otherwise healthy.

prompt: Which global configuration command starts an IPv6 static route?
options: ip route
ipv6 route
route ipv6
ipv6 static
explanation: IPv6 static routes use ipv6 route followed by prefix/length.

whyWrong.0: ip route configures IPv4 static routes.
whyWrong.2: route ipv6 is not an IOS command.
whyWrong.3: ipv6 static is not an IOS command.

prompt: What does IPv6 use on Ethernet to find the MAC address of a next hop?
options: Address Resolution Protocol (ARP)
Stateful DHCPv6 server lookup
Neighbor Discovery
RIPng routing updates
explanation: IPv6 uses Neighbor Discovery in place of ARP.

whyWrong.0: ARP is used with IPv4.
whyWrong.1: DHCPv6 assigns configuration, not MAC addresses.
whyWrong.3: RIPng is a routing protocol.

prompt: How must a floating static route's administrative distance compare with the preferred route to the same prefix?
options: Lower
Higher
Equal
It does not matter
explanation: A floating route needs a higher administrative distance so it is installed only when the preferred route is gone.

whyWrong.0: A lower distance would make it the preferred route.
whyWrong.2: An equal distance would load-share, not stand by.
whyWrong.3: The distance decides which route is installed.

prompt: What administrative distance does an ordinary static route have by default?
explanation: An ordinary static route has administrative distance 1.

whyWrong.0: 0 is a connected interface.
whyWrong.2: 90 is EIGRP.
whyWrong.3: 110 is OSPF.
